assembly_instructions: Presentation diorama, modelled at 0.6x of real metres (facts[] quote full-scale metres). Right-handed, +Y up. The single concrete ground plate spans X and Z and is framed by a four-member raised brushed-steel perimeter curb; a raised 0.36 m brushed-steel curb wall along X at z=0 splits it into two halves. LEFT HALF (z>0) is the VISIBLE physical city: eight steel/concrete/glass towers, four set on concrete podiums, all eight crowned with rooftop mechanical units, the two tallest also carrying lattice masts; the three glass towers and the concrete mid-rise Building 5 are each banded by three exposed brushed-steel floor slabs so storeys are visible. Two intersecting flat-box roads carry centre lane markings; a short bridge sits on two piers and two streetlights line the main road. RIGHT HALF (z<0) is the INVISIBLE digital city rebuilt from infrastructure: eight 19-inch racks at the mirror image (same X, negated Z) of the eight buildings so the urban footprint is preserved. Each rack is built as an OPEN 4-post 19-inch cabinet — a left side panel, a right side panel, two front and two rear mounting posts and a top frame cap — with three brushed-steel server-blade units mounted in the open front bay so the rack visibly reads as populated. A data-center spine runs along X, three brushed-steel network-node towers carry an overhead copper backbone, eight copper data links drop one rack each into the spine, and a cross data conduit mirrors the physical cross road. Build order: lay the ground plate and bolt on the perimeter curb frame; set the divider curb wall; cast the four podiums and erect the eight buildings; band the three glass towers and Building 5 with their floor slabs; cap every building with a rooftop mechanical unit and the two tallest with masts; lay the roads and paint the lane markings; raise the bridge piers and deck; plant the streetlights; on the digital half, for each rack erect the left then right side panel, drop in the lower/mid/upper blade units, fit the two front and two rear mounting posts and the top frame cap; lay the data-center spine and the cross conduit; raise the three network towers; string the overhead backbone; run the eight copper data links. The connection graph is rooted at the ground plate. The layout is fully open — nothing is enclosed — and is intended to be viewed from a 3/4 angle.

info.japanese_name: 二都市ジオラマ（実体都市とデジタル都市）
info.english_name: Two-Cities Diorama (Physical City vs. Digital Twin)
info.summary: A split-plate diorama that places a small physical city beside its digital-infrastructure twin, where every building has a mirrored counterpart rebuilt from an open 4-post 19-inch server rack and a copper network. It visualises how the same urban footprint exists simultaneously as steel-and-concrete and as data.
info.description: The diorama sits on one 16 m x 11 m concrete ground plate framed by a raised brushed-steel perimeter curb and divided by a raised brushed-steel curb wall; it is modelled at 0.6x so it stays within a compact viewing radius. The left half is a conventional skyline: eight buildings between 2.5 m and 6.0 m tall in concrete, welded steel and blue glass curtain wall, the four prominent towers set on concrete ground-floor podiums, all eight crowned with rooftop mechanical units and the two tallest also carrying lattice masts; the three glass towers and the concrete mid-rise Building 5 are banded by exposed brushed-steel floor slabs so individual storeys read clearly. Two roads with painted centre lines, a small bridge and streetlights complete the street scene. The right half is the 'invisible city' — the identical street footprint is mirrored across the divider, but each building is replaced by an open 4-post 19-inch server rack (0.6 m wide, 1.0 m deep) of the same relative height, built as a framed cabinet — two side panels, two front and two rear mounting posts and a top cap — so its interior is exposed. Each rack carries three discrete brushed-steel server-blade units in its open front bay so the rack reads as populated. A 14 m data-center spine threads the racks together, a cross conduit mirrors the physical cross road, three brushed-steel network-node towers carry an overhead copper backbone, and eight copper data links drop each rack into the spine. The piece is a teaching prop for a presentation slide, so it is deliberately open: no enclosures, no roofs, every component visible from a 3/4 camera.
